title: DMC3 HD indexed data arrays, and why the name runs are not among them

records.title: The decoder's addressing fields agree with an independent disassembler everywhere
records.summary: Following a table base through a register needs the base, index and scale of a memory operand, which the length decoder parsed and discarded. Surfacing them changes no length logic: REX.R, REX.X and REX.B extend the register numbers, a SIB index of four without REX.X is the encoding for no index while with REX.X it is r12, and a SIB base of five under mod zero is a bare displacement with no base at all. Every indexed memory operand in the image was then compared against objdump: 16,503 operands, complete agreement on base, index and scale. The 56 not compared are objdump's riz pseudo-register, which is the no-index encoding the decoder reports as having no index, and 32-bit addressing forms.

locations.symbol: executable section cross-validated for addressing operands
locations.note: 16,503 indexed memory operands compared against objdump, agreement on base, index and scale in every case.

records.title: The image base is held in a register and indexed against
records.summary: A bounded walk that remembers what a RIP-relative lea put into a register, and gives it up on any instruction naming that register, on every call and after sixty-four instructions, finds 1,303 indexed reads whose base it can name. 749 of them hold RVA zero, which is the image base: MSVC emits lea against __ImageBase and then reaches a table by displacement alone. The function at RVA 0x31650 shows the whole form, loading the image base into r13 and reading a table of eight-byte elements at RVA 0x5E1668 with a scaled index. This is the same construct the switch-table recovery relies on, now readable for data tables generally rather than inferred from a candidate list.

table read against the image base

records.title: No recovered name run or record is indexed as an array
records.summary: Of 1,303 indexed reads whose base the walk can name, not one reaches a recovered run or record at its own element size. The four whose base register holds a run's base exactly are all the inlined string scan, base plus index times one minus one, walking the first name's characters. Every other access into a run's bytes loads one element's address outright. The runs are therefore a layout fact about how the linker packed these literals, not an access fact about how the game reads them, and the fixed stride is the packer's alignment rather than an array's element size. The evidence is strong where a stride is eight, because a scale of eight is then the natural encoding and 211 such reads exist elsewhere in the image; it was weaker above eight until the index multiplier was carried through, and now holds for every stride the walk can name: 155 arrays are walked with a scaled index, with element sizes up to 72 bytes, and not one of them is a recovered run.

locations.note: RVA 0x35D4B8, stride 8, sample name .PSS. Eight sites reach its elements, each an inlined character scan of an address loaded outright.

records.title: An element size above eight is carried in the index, not the scale
records.summary: A SIB scale encodes only one, two, four and eight, so an array of any other element size is reached by multiplying the index before the read: lea reg with base and index the same register multiplies by two, three, five or nine, imul by a constant multiplies by it, and a shift by a constant multiplies by a power of two. The image holds 933 of the lea form alone. Carrying that multiplier through to the read makes those element sizes visible, and 40 reads then show sizes of 6, 10, 12, 20, 24, 40 and 72 bytes that no scale field could have expressed. This closes the half of the earlier finding that was weak: the absence of indexed access to a name run is now measured for every stride, not only for eight.

records.title: 155 arrays in data are walked with a scaled index, and their element layout is partly readable
records.summary: Of 554 indexed reads on a base other than the image base, 267 have a displacement that lands inside the element, which is what a field offset must do. 255 have a negative displacement and are the inlined character scan over a string rather than an array walk. 32 sit at or past the element, meaning the element size or the base is wrong there, and that 5.8 per cent is the error bar on the inference rather than something to hide. What survives is 155 arrays, of which 28 are read at more than one offset within their element and so carry a partial layout rather than a single observation: the array at RVA 0x5D08A0 has a 20-byte element read at four offsets, and the one at RVA 0x570600 a 12-byte element read at three. All of this is layout recovered from instruction encodings; no contents are read.

records.title: The sites that failed the consistency check named the step that was missing
records.summary: Thirty-two reads had a field offset at or past the element the walk computed, and they were not noise. The function at RVA 0x274730 shows what they were: a base loaded into r14, then lea with base and index the same register to multiply by five, then add of the register to itself to double it, then a read scaled by eight. Eighty bytes. The doubling was the step the multiplier tracking did not model, so the element read as forty and every field offset from eight to twenty-eight fell outside it. Adding the self-add form, and the shift form alongside it, takes inconsistent reads from 32 to 16 and consistent array walks from 267 to 304. The array at RVA 0x597150 now reads as an eighty-byte element with eight four-byte fields, which is what the instructions say it is. The check earned its keep twice over: it flagged the gap, and the gap named the instruction form to add.

records.title: Five bases are read at two element sizes, which cannot both be right
records.summary: Grouping by base and element size leaves 173 arrays over 168 distinct bases, so five bases carry two readings apiece. A base cannot have two element sizes, so at least one reading of each is wrong, and nothing in the encodings says which. Reporting the count rather than picking a winner keeps the contradiction visible: three per cent of bases, alongside the sixteen reads whose field offset still falls outside its element.

locations.symbol: base read at two element sizes
locations.note: RVA 0x596DE0, read as a 48-byte element at six sites and as an 8-byte element at one.

records.title: Grouping image-base reads by address proximity would have invented layouts
records.summary: An image-base read folds the array's start into the displacement, so one read cannot separate base from field. Grouping reads whose addresses lie within one element of each other looked like the way to recover those layouts, and would have produced eighteen arrays. Grouping instead by what is actually shared — one function, one index register, one element size — shows why that is unsound: of the 60 such groups holding more than one read, 53 span more than one element, meaning the register was reused for a different array. Only 7 are one array's fields, and two of those reproduce a base and element size a register was separately seen holding, which corroborates both routes. The measurement of the false-merge rate is the result here; the seven layouts are recorded with their base marked as an upper bound, since the array may begin before the lowest address observed.

locations.note: RVA 0x4E9020, element 8 bytes, fields at +0 and +4, seen both through a register holding the base and through image-base reads sharing an index register.
RVA 0xD6CB54, element 24 bytes, fields at +0, +4 and +12 relative to the lowest address observed, which bounds the array's start from above.

records.title: Correction: the element-size conflicts were resolvable, and reading them halved the error bar
records.summary: Bases read at more than one element size were published as a contradiction with nothing to say which reading was wrong, and reported rather than resolved. Reading them shows the structure does say which. A multiplier is recorded only off a definite lea, imul or shl, so it can be missed but never invented, and an element size equal to the raw SIB scale is one read with no multiplier seen. Across all eleven such bases in the image the smaller reading both divides the larger and equals its own scale — eleven of eleven, no exceptions — which is a missed multiplier rather than a second array. Resolving to the larger reading halves the count of accesses whose displacement falls outside its element, from 28 to 14, and raises consistent accesses from 541 to 555 by exactly those 14. The base at RVA 0x580D20 reads as a 24-byte record with fields at 0, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 where it was previously an 8-byte reading plus accesses reported as inconsistent. A base whose sizes do not divide is still a real conflict and is now left out of the layout entirely rather than given a size it may not have; there are none in this image, and a test covers the case.
